chapter: Young players, schools and studio work
title: Trumbauer, Bix and Lloyd Reese's advice
summary: Maxwell and Hinton recall Frank Trumbauer; Maxwell never liked Bix, though Lloyd Reese urged him to learn from him.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Bix Beiderbecke: hearing, copying and remembering him

blocks.x: Yeah, right. Thank you for your great defense. I think that's good. We're sitting on opposite sides of the fence and I'm on the side you're talking about, only as a senior citizen now. But I'm concerned with -- I've listened to Prez, when he was living, talk about how he was influenced by some great white players like the great saxophone player that was with Paul Whiteman's band that played C melody saxophone.
Yeah, I keep thinking Teschma ker
It wasn't Teschma ker. It was the guy who recorded with Bix Beiderbecke all the time.
Yeah, I can't recall his name right now.
It's terrible, I can't think of his name, either.
I have known Trumbauer what an excellent musician he was, and he really did, if you think about it --

Oh, yeah, I do believe it, yes. I do believe that. And I like Trumbauer myself. That's one of the few musicians from that circle -- I never liked Bix Beiderbecke. I never understood what the hollering was all about. And the funny thing, the first person that made me see any value at all, was Lloyd Reese, a black trumpet player. And he said, don't put him down just because he doesn't sound like Louis Armstrong. He said, there's a lot to learn from him. And he pointed it out but at that time I couldn't see it. Now, of course, I can see some value. But I still can't say truthfully -- that impresses me.
